<a id="pm-s1"></a>
## 1. Abstract and result contract

> We prove that every finite nonempty graph <i>G</i> satisfies $`\chi_{\mathrm{list}}(G)\le C h(G)`$ for an absolute integer <i>C</i>, where $`h(G)`$ is the largest order of a clique minor. This resolves the Linear List Hadwiger conjecture affirmatively.

- **claim-thm-main** (theorem, [source](#stmt-thm-main)): There is an absolute integer $C\ge1$ such that every finite nonempty simple graph $G$ satisfies $$\ell(G)\le C h(G).$$
  - Explanation: An absolute coefficient bounds list chromatic number by clique-minor order uniformly over finite nonempty simple graphs.
- **claim-cor-ordinary** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-cor-ordinary)): Every finite nonempty simple graph $G$ satisfies $\chi(G)\le C h(G)$, with the constant $C$ in Theorem <a href="#thm:main" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:main">1</a>.
  - Explanation: Using a common list gives the corresponding ordinary chromatic bound.
- **claim-thm-fractional** (theorem, [source](#stmt-thm-fractional)): Every graph $P$ satisfies $f(P)\le4h(P)$.
  - Explanation: Fractional coloring has a linear minor-order bound.
- **claim-thm-ordinary-extraction** (theorem, [source](#stmt-thm-ordinary-extraction)): If $k\ge1$ is an integer and $\chi(P)\ge7k$, then $P$ has a $k$-connected subgraph $J$ with $\chi(J)\ge\chi(P)-6k$.
  - Explanation: Large ordinary chromatic number yields a highly connected subgraph with controlled chromatic loss.
- **claim-thm-grouping** (theorem, [source](#stmt-thm-grouping)): There is an absolute integer $\gamma\ge1$ such that the following holds. In a $\gamma m$-connected graph, every partition of $m\ge1$ distinct terminals into nonempty groups can be realized by pairwise disjoint connected vertex sets, one containing each group.
  - Explanation: Sufficient connectivity realizes prescribed terminal groups in disjoint connected sets.
- **claim-lem-bounded** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-lem-bounded)): Suppose $\|V(P)\|\le n$, where $n\ge1$, and $f(P)\le r$, where $r\ge1$. There is a distribution on stable sets $I$ such that $$\|I\|\le\lceil n/r\rceil, \qquad \Pr(v\in I)=\frac1{2r}\quad(v\in V(P)).$$
  - Explanation: Stable sets can be sampled with bounded size and equal vertex marginals.
- **claim-lem-concentration** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-lem-concentration)): Let $Z$ be a function of $s\ge1$ independent finite random variables. If changing one variable changes $Z$ by at most $b>0$, then $$\Pr\bigl(\|Z-\mathbb EZ\|\ge u\bigr) \le2\exp\bigl(-u^2/(2sb^2)\bigr)\qquad(u>0).$$
  - Explanation: Independent finite trials with bounded changes give exponential concentration.
- **claim-lem-cut-test** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-lem-cut-test)): Let $P$ be a $k$-connected graph on at most $n$ vertices, where $k$ is a sufficiently large integer. Set $$s=\left\lceil10(n/k)\log(2n)\right\rceil.$$ There is a family of at most $(n+1)^{s+1}$ matchings, each of size $\lfloor k/8\rfloor$, with the following property. If $U\subseteq V(P)$, every vertex of $P$ has at least $k/2$ neighbors outside $U$, and fewer than $k/32$ endpoints of each matching belong to $U$, then $P-U$ is $\lfloor k/32\rfloor$-connected.
  - Explanation: A fixed matching family and surviving neighbor counts certify connectivity after deletion.
- **claim-prop-small-list** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-prop-small-list)): There are an absolute positive integer $L$ and an absolute integer $t_0$ such that, for every integer $t\ge t_0$ and every graph $G$, $$h(G)<t,\qquad \|V(G)\|\le t^{11/10} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \ell(G)\le Lt.$$
  - Explanation: Minor exclusion gives a linear list bound in the stated small-order regime.
- **claim-small-eligible-thinning** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-small-eligible-thinning)): There is an absolute positive integer $B$ such that the following holds for all sufficiently large integers $t$. Let $n,r$ be real parameters with $$1\le n\le t^{11/10},\qquad \frac{t}{\log t}\le r\le4t,$$ and let $P$ be a graph with $\|V(P)\|\le n$, $h(P)<t$, and $f(P)\le r$. Set $$N=\left\lceil Br\log\bigl(2\max\{1,t/r\}\bigr)\right\rceil.$$ Suppose $E_1,\ldots,E_N\subseteq V(P)$ contain every vertex at least $N/2$ times. There are stable sets $I_1,\ldots,I_N$ of $P$, each of size at most $\lceil n/r\rceil$, such that $$f\left(P-\bigcup_{j=1}^N(I_j\cap E_j)\right)\le r/2.$$ The cutoff for $t$ is uniform over $P,n,r$ and the eligibility sets.
  - Explanation: Eligibility restrictions fixed before sampling still permit fractional-chromatic halving.
- **claim-small-concentration** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-small-concentration)): Take at most $q$ independent copies of the experiment <a href="#small:remainder" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="small:remainder">[small:remainder]</a>. Let $Z$ be any one of the following quantities, where the vertex set $A\subseteq V(P)$ is fixed before sampling: $$\|A\cap W_i\|,\qquad \left\|A\cap\bigcup_iW_i\right\|,\qquad f(P[A\cap W_i]).$$ For each fixed $\delta>0$, and all sufficiently large $t$, $$\label{small:uniform-tail} \Pr\bigl(\|Z-\mathbb EZ\|\ge\delta r\bigr) \le2\exp(-t^{7/10}),$$ uniformly over all the data in <a href="#small:range" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="small:range">[small:range]</a> and all eligibility sets satisfying the stated condition.
  - Explanation: Remainder counts and fractional chromatic numbers concentrate uniformly in the stated regime.
- **claim-small-fixed-region** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-small-fixed-region)): Suppose that every outcome of the experiment <a href="#small:remainder" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="small:remainder">[small:remainder]</a> having positive probability satisfies $f(P[W])>r/2$. Then there is a fixed induced $k$-connected subgraph $H\subseteq P$ such that $$\label{small:region-expectation} \mathbb E f(H[W\cap V(H)])>r/4.$$ The subgraph $H$ is chosen before any fresh copies of the experiment are sampled.
  - Explanation: Failure of every thinning outcome localizes expected fractional chromatic number in a fixed highly connected region.
- **claim-small-private** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-small-private)): With failure probability at most $4q(q-1)p+o(1)$, every $H[T_i]$ has fractional chromatic number greater than $r/8$, and hence contains a $K_{2x}$ model.
  - Explanation: Private subsets from independent remainders retain enough fractional chromatic number to support disjoint clique models.
- **claim-small-complement** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-small-complement)): With probability $1-o(1)$, every vertex of $H$ has at least $k/2$ neighbors in $H-U$, and $H-U$ is $\lfloor k/32\rfloor$-connected.
  - Explanation: The sampled complement retains neighborhood supply and high connectivity.
- **claim-lem-list-extraction** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-lem-list-extraction)): For every integer $k\ge1$, if $\ell(P)>6k$, then some induced $k$-connected subgraph $H$ of $P$ satisfies $$\ell(H)\ge\ell(P)-6k.$$
  - Explanation: Large list chromatic number yields an induced highly connected subgraph with controlled loss.
- **claim-list-high-neighbor-count** (bound, [source](#stmt-list-high-neighbor-count)): Let $t\ge2$ be an integer, let $h(P)<t$, and let $X\subseteq V(P)$. Then $$\bigl\|\{v\in V(P)\setminus X:\|N_P(v)\cap X\|\ge t\}\bigr\| \le\binom{\|X\|}{2}.$$
  - Explanation: Minor exclusion bounds outside vertices having many neighbors in a fixed set.
- **claim-lem-coarse-density** (bound, [source](#stmt-lem-coarse-density)): There is an absolute constant $C_*>0$, for example $C_*=10^4$, such that, for every integer $t\ge2$ and every nonempty graph $P$ with $h(P)<t$, $$d(P)\le C_*t\log(2t).$$ Consequently, every graph $P$ with $h(P)<t$ satisfies $$\ell(P)\le 2C_*t\log(2t)+1.$$
  - Explanation: Minor exclusion bounds density and consequently gives a degeneracy-based list bound.
- **claim-lem-incidence** (bound, [source](#stmt-lem-incidence)): There is an absolute positive integer $B_*$ such that, for all sufficiently large integers $t$, every graph $P$ with $h(P)<t$ and disjoint vertex sets $A,T$ satisfies $$\label{density:incidence-bound} \sum_{\substack{v\in T\\ \|N_P(v)\cap A\|\ge B_*t}} \|N_P(v)\cap A\| \le t^{1+2\epsilon}\|A\|.$$ In particular, $$\bigl\|\{v\in T:\|N_P(v)\cap A\|\ge B_*t\}\bigr\| \le t^{2\epsilon}\|A\|.$$
  - Explanation: Minor exclusion controls the total incidence of vertices with many neighbors in a fixed disjoint set.
- **claim-density-connectivity** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-density-connectivity)): For every positive integer $k$, a graph of density greater than $2k$ contains an induced $k$-connected subgraph.
  - Explanation: Sufficient density yields an induced highly connected subgraph.
- **claim-lem-district** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-lem-district)): For every fixed positive integer $K$, there is an integer $$D_K>\max(400B_*,12800K)$$ such that, for all sufficiently large integers $t$, every nonempty graph $P$ with $$h(P)<t,\qquad d(P)\ge D_Kt$$ contains an induced $(Kt)$-connected subgraph of order at most $t^{1.06}$.
  - Explanation: Sufficient density in a minor-free graph yields a small highly connected induced district.
- **claim-density-list-district** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-density-list-district)): Fix $K$ and $D_K$ as in Lemma <a href="#lem:district" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:district">23</a>. For all sufficiently large integers $t$, if $$h(P)<t,\qquad \ell(P)>2D_Kt+2,$$ then $P$ contains an induced $(Kt)$-connected subgraph of order at most $t^{1.06}$.
  - Explanation: Large list chromatic number forces a small highly connected district under minor exclusion.
- **claim-lem-packing** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-lem-packing)): Let $A,B$ be disjoint vertex sets in a graph $P$, and let $j\ge1$ be an integer. Suppose that for every $X\subseteq V(P)$ with $\|X\|<j$, the graph $P-X$ contains a path from $A\setminus X$ to $B\setminus X$. Then there are $j$ pairwise vertex-disjoint paths from distinct vertices of $A$ to distinct vertices of $B$. Each path can be chosen to meet $A\cup B$ only at its two ends.
  - Explanation: The absence of a small vertex separator yields disjoint source-to-target paths.
- **claim-lem-double-packing** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-lem-double-packing)): Let $A,B$ be disjoint vertex sets in a graph $P$, where $r=\|A\|\ge1$. If $P$ is $2r$-connected and $\|B\|\ge2r$, there are two paths starting at each vertex of $A$, ending at $2r$ distinct vertices of $B$, with no intersections other than the two paths sharing their prescribed start. Their internal vertices lie outside $A\cup B$.
  - Explanation: Connectivity supports doubled routes from every source with distinct target ends.
- **claim-lem-rooting** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-lem-rooting)): Let $k\ge1$. If $P$ is $2k$-connected and $h(P)\ge4k$, then any given $k$ distinct vertices are roots of a $K_k$ model: its bags can be indexed by the given vertices so that each bag contains its indexing root.
  - Explanation: A sufficiently large clique model and sufficient connectivity allow arbitrary prescribed roots.
- **claim-lem-small-woven** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-lem-small-woven)): For all sufficiently large integers $t$, every $(K_0t)$-connected graph $J$ of order at most $t^{1.06}$ is $(s,3t)$-woven whenever $$1\le s\le 2\left\lceil\frac{t}{(\log t)^2}\right\rceil.$$ The cutoff is absolute and uniform in $s$ and $J$. No minor-exclusion hypothesis on $J$ is required.
  - Explanation: Small highly connected districts simultaneously support rooted models and prescribed paths.
- **claim-lem-separability** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-lem-separability)): There is an absolute positive integer $S$ such that, for all sufficiently large integers $t$, every graph $G$ satisfying $$h(G)<t,\qquad r=\ell(G)\ge 2St$$ has two vertex-disjoint induced subgraphs $G_1,G_2$ with $$\ell(G_1),\ell(G_2)\ge r-St.$$
  - Explanation: A minor-free graph with sufficiently large list chromatic number splits into disjoint induced subgraphs retaining nearly all of it.
- **claim-thm-recursive-woven** (theorem, [source](#stmt-thm-recursive-woven)): There are absolute positive integers $K,Q$ such that, for every integer $a\ge1$, every $Ka$-connected graph $P$ with $\ell(P)\ge Qa$ is $(a,3a)$-woven.
  - Explanation: Linear connectivity and list-chromatic thresholds imply simultaneous rooted-model and path routing.
- **claim-list-elementary** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-list-elementary)): The following hold for every finite graph $P$.* 1. *If $H$ is a subgraph of $P$, then $\ell(H)\le \ell(P)$.* 2. *For every $Z\subseteq V(P)$, $$\ell(P-Z)\ge \ell(P)-\|Z\|.$$* 3. *If $P$ is $q$-degenerate, where $q$ is a nonnegative integer, then $\ell(P)\le q+1$.
  - Explanation: List chromatic number is monotone under subgraphs, loses at most the deleted vertex count, and is bounded by degeneracy.
- **claim-list-constrained-coloring** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-list-constrained-coloring)): Let $k\ge1$ and $m\ge0$ be integers. Suppose every induced $k$-connected subgraph of $P$ has list chromatic number at most $m$. Give each vertex $v$ a list $\mathcal L(v)$ of size at least $m+6k$. Suppose also that:* 1. *a set $A\subseteq V(P)$ has a proper list precoloring $\varphi$;* 2. *for each $v\notin A$, a finite set $B_v$ of forbidden colors is specified, with $\|B_v\|<k$;* 3. *the constraints satisfy $$\label{list:eq-budget} k\|A\|+\sum_{v\notin A}\|B_v\|\le2k^2.$$* *Then $P$ has a proper $\mathcal L$-coloring extending $\varphi$ and avoiding $B_v$ at every $v\notin A$.
  - Explanation: A constraint budget permits extension of a list precoloring while respecting forbidden colors.
- **claim-lem-additive-deletion** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-lem-additive-deletion)): Let $L\ge1$ be the integer constant in Proposition <a href="#prop:small-list" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:small-list">9</a>. For each fixed integer $d\ge0$, put $$c_d=4L+d+5.$$ For every sufficiently large integer $t$, the following holds. Suppose $h(P)<t$ and $X,Y\subseteq V(P)$ are disjoint sets such that* 1. *$\|X\|\le t^{11/10}$;* 2. *$P[Y]$ is $dt$-degenerate;* 3. *every vertex outside $X\cup Y$ has at most $dt$ neighbors in $Y$.* *Then $$\ell(P-X-Y)\ge\ell(P)-c_dt.$$ The cutoff is independent of $P$, its order, and all list assignments and their palettes.
  - Explanation: Deleting a small set and a suitably sparse set incurs only linear list-chromatic loss under minor exclusion.
- **claim-lem-rerouting** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-lem-rerouting)): Let $J$ be an $(a,b)$-woven subgraph of a graph $P$, and prescribe $a$ distinct roots in $J$. Let $Q_1,\ldots,Q_q$ be vertex-disjoint paths in $P$, where $q\le b$. Orient each path arbitrarily. For every path meeting $J$, let $x_i,y_i$ be its first and last vertices in $J$. There are vertex-disjoint paths $Q'_1,\ldots,Q'_q$ with the same respective endpoints, and a model rooted at the prescribed roots in $J$, such that the following properties hold:* 1. *every vertex added to a path belongs to $J$; more precisely, $V(Q'_i)\setminus V(J)\subseteq V(Q_i)\setminus V(J)$;* 2. *a path originally disjoint from $J$ is unchanged;* 3. *the intersection of $Q'_i$ with the model is contained in the prescribed roots among $x_i,y_i$.* *The construction can be applied successively in disjoint districts. If some prescribed roots are endpoints of the original path system, the bags for these roots meet the resulting paths only at their own roots, including after all subsequent replacements in other districts.
  - Explanation: Woven districts allow path replacement and rooted model insertion with the specified intersection guarantees.
- **claim-lem-path-minimization** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-lem-path-minimization)): Let $A,B$ be disjoint vertex sets in a graph $P$. Suppose that a system of one of the two types above is feasible, and choose one of minimum total length. Let $q$ be its number of paths and $U$ its vertex union. Then:* 1. *the paths have no internal vertices in $A\cup B$;* 2. *each vertex of $V(P)\setminus U$ has at most three neighbors on any one path;* 3. *$P[U\setminus A]$ is $2q$-degenerate for type <span class="upright">(1)</span>, and $P[U]$ is $2q$-degenerate for type <span class="upright">(2)</span>.
  - Explanation: Free endpoint assignments and minimum total length give external-neighbor and degeneracy bounds.
- **claim-lem-combine** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-lem-combine)): Let $Z,D,V(H)$ be pairwise disjoint vertex sets in a graph $P$, and let $m\ge1$. Suppose there are:* 1. *two paths from each vertex of $Z$ to distinct vertices of $D$, with all target ends distinct, with intersections only at their prescribed repeated starts, and avoiding $V(H)$;* 2. *$2m$ vertex-disjoint paths from distinct vertices of $H$ to distinct vertices of $D$, avoiding $Z$ and meeting $H$ only at their starting vertices.* *Then, using only vertices of these two families, one can obtain $\|Z\|+m$ vertex-disjoint paths to distinct vertices of $D$, one starting at each vertex of $Z$ and one starting at each of $m$ distinct vertices of $H$. These paths meet $D$ and $H$ only at their appropriate ends. Moreover, after any partition of the $2m$ second-family starts into $m$ pairs, the $m$ selected starts in $H$ can be required to include exactly one vertex from each pair. No unselected second-family start is visited by any of the resulting paths.
  - Explanation: Doubled path families can be combined while selecting a source from each prescribed pair.
- **claim-separate-footprint** (conditional_result, [source](#stmt-separate-footprint)): Let $h(G)<t$. Start with $F_0=W_0$, where $\|W_0\|=t$, and perform at most $R_t$ rounds with the following rules. At the start of a round there is a footprint $F$ and a set $W\subseteq F$ of $t$ tips.* 1. *Choose disjoint sets $J,D\subseteq V(G)\setminus F$, each of size at most $t^{1.06}$, and a set $R\subseteq J$ of at most $t$ vertices. Put $Z=W\cup R$.* 2. *In the induced graph $G-(F\setminus W)$, choose a minimum-total-length double system $\mathcal Q_1$ from $Z$ to $D$: two paths from each vertex of $Z$, otherwise vertex-disjoint, with distinct target ends. Set $$F^- =F\cup J\cup D\cup V(\mathcal Q_1).$$* 3. *Choose a source set $A\subseteq V(G)\setminus F^-$. In the induced graph $G-(F\cup R)$, choose a minimum-total-length system $\mathcal Q_2$ of $2t$ vertex-disjoint paths from arbitrary distinct vertices of $A$ to arbitrary distinct vertices of $D$. Set $$F^+=F^-\cup V(\mathcal Q_2),$$ and choose $t$ tips $W^+\subseteq F^+$ for the next round.* *Only histories in which the indicated systems exist are considered. The final round may end after step <span class="upright">(ii)</span>.* *There is an absolute integer $$\label{separate:cf} c_f=c_{6B_*+20}=4L+6B_*+25$$ such that, for all sufficiently large $t$, every final footprint $F_{\rm last}$ of such a history satisfies $$\ell(G-F_{\rm last})\ge\ell(G)-c_ft.$$ The same assertion holds for the initial footprint.
  - Explanation: The whole recorded path history has controlled additive list-chromatic deletion cost, independent of path lengths.

        }

        "anchor": "stmt-list-constrained-coloring",
        "exact_quote": "Let $k\\ge1$ and $m\\ge0$ be integers. Suppose every induced $k$-connected subgraph of $P$ has list chromatic number at most $m$. Give each vertex $v$ a list $\\mathcal L(v)$ of size at least $m+6k$. Suppose also that:*\n\n1.  *a set $A\\subseteq V(P)$ has a proper list precoloring $\\varphi$;*\n\n2.  *for each $v\\notin A$, a finite set $B_v$ of forbidden colors is specified, with $|B_v|<k$;*\n\n3.  *the constraints satisfy $$\\label{list:eq-budget}\n    k|A|+\\sum_{v\\notin A}|B_v|\\le2k^2.$$*\n\n*Then $P$ has a proper $\\mathcal L$-coloring extending $\\varphi$ and avoiding $B_v$ at every $v\\notin A$.",

        "anchor": "stmt-lem-rerouting",
        "exact_quote": "Let $J$ be an $(a,b)$-woven subgraph of a graph $P$, and prescribe $a$ distinct roots in $J$. Let $Q_1,\\ldots,Q_q$ be vertex-disjoint paths in $P$, where $q\\le b$. Orient each path arbitrarily. For every path meeting $J$, let $x_i,y_i$ be its first and last vertices in $J$. There are vertex-disjoint paths $Q'_1,\\ldots,Q'_q$ with the same respective endpoints, and a model rooted at the prescribed roots in $J$, such that the following properties hold:*\n\n1.  *every vertex added to a path belongs to $J$; more precisely, $V(Q'_i)\\setminus V(J)\\subseteq V(Q_i)\\setminus V(J)$;*\n\n2.  *a path originally disjoint from $J$ is unchanged;*\n\n3.  *the intersection of $Q'_i$ with the model is contained in the prescribed roots among $x_i,y_i$.*\n\n*The construction can be applied successively in disjoint districts.         "anchor": "stmt-lem-combine",
        "exact_quote": "Let $Z,D,V(H)$ be pairwise disjoint vertex sets in a graph $P$, and let $m\\ge1$. Suppose there are:*\n\n1.  *two paths from each vertex of $Z$ to distinct vertices of $D$, with all target ends distinct, with intersections only at their prescribed repeated starts, and avoiding $V(H)$;*\n\n2.  *$2m$ vertex-disjoint paths from distinct vertices of $H$ to distinct vertices of $D$, avoiding $Z$ and meeting $H$ only at their starting vertices.*\n\n*Then, using only vertices of these two families, one can obtain $|Z|+m$ vertex-disjoint paths to distinct vertices of $D$, one starting at each vertex of $Z$ and one starting at each of $m$ distinct vertices of $H$. These paths meet $D$ and $H$ only at their appropriate ends. Moreover, after any partition of the $2m$ second-family starts into $m$ pairs, the $m$ selected starts in $H$ can be required to include exactly one vertex from each pair. <a id="pm-s2"></a>
## 2. Definitions, validity and bounds

- **list assignment** ([source](#sec:introduction)): A *list assignment* $\mathcal L$ assigns a finite set of colors to each vertex.
- **list coloring** ([source](#sec:introduction)): An $\mathcal L$-coloring is a proper coloring $c$ satisfying $c(v)\in\mathcal L(v)$ at every vertex.
- **list chromatic number** ([source](#sec:introduction)): The list chromatic number $\ell(G)=\chi_{\mathrm{list}}(G)$ is the least integer $k$ for which every assignment with $\|\mathcal L(v)\|\ge k$ is colorable.
- **Hadwiger number** ([source](#sec:introduction)): For a finite nonempty simple graph $G$, let $h(G)$ be the largest order of a clique minor in $G$.
- **stable set** ([source](#sec:preliminaries)): A *stable set* is a set of pairwise nonadjacent vertices.
- **clique model** ([source](#sec:preliminaries)): A clique model consists of disjoint nonempty connected vertex sets, called *bags*, with an edge between every two bags.
- **vertex connectivity** ([source](#sec:preliminaries)): A graph is $k$-connected if it has more than $k$ vertices and remains connected after deletion of fewer than $k$ vertices.
- **fractional chromatic number** ([source](#pm-h-6)): The fractional chromatic number $f(P)$ is the minimum total weight of nonnegative weights on the stable sets of $P$ that cover every vertex with weight at least one.
- **density** ([source](#sec:density)): Write $e(R)=\|E(R)\|$ and $d(R)=e(R)/\|V(R)\|$ for a nonempty graph $R$.
- **woven graph** ([source](#stmt-def-woven)): For integers $a\ge1$ and $b\ge0$, a graph $J$ is *$(a,b)$-woven* if the following holds. Prescribe $a$ distinct roots $R=\{r_1,\ldots,r_a\}$ and at most $b$ pairs $(x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_p,y_p)$ of vertices of $J$. The endpoint sets $\{x_i,y_i\}$ must be disjoint for different $i$, but $x_i=y_i$ is allowed, and endpoints may belong to $R$. Then there are a $K_a$ model with bags $M_1,\ldots,M_a$ satisfying $r_j\in M_j$, and pairwise vertex-disjoint $x_i$–$y_i$ paths $Q_i$, such that $$V(Q_i)\cap\bigcup_{j=1}^a M_j \ \subseteq\ R\cap\{x_i,y_i\}\qquad(1\le i\le p).$$ For a coincident pair the path is the single prescribed vertex. Because the model bags are disjoint and contain all the roots, any allowed intersection at $r_j$ belongs to the designated bag $M_j$.

<a id="pm-s3"></a>
## 3. Proof roadmap

- **sampling** [claim](#stmt-lem-bounded) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-bounded): Thin a stable-set distribution and split its sampled sets into bounded parts. -> Bounded stable-set marginals
- **small** [claim](#stmt-prop-small-list) / [proof](#proof-stmt-small-complement-3): Partition colors globally into bins, thin eligible stable sets, and cover the remainder. -> Small-graph list coloring
- **extraction** [claim](#stmt-lem-list-extraction) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-list-extraction): Apply constraint-budget coloring contrapositively. -> Highly connected induced region
- **deletion** [claim](#stmt-lem-additive-deletion) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-additive-deletion): Reserve colors globally and prune only colors used on previously colored neighbors. -> Controlled additive list-chromatic loss
- **districts** [claim](#stmt-lem-district) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-district): Use maximal contractions under an edge-loss budget to find a small dense neighborhood. -> Small highly connected district
- **separability** [claim](#stmt-lem-separability) / [proof](#proof-stmt-separate-footprint-2): Record minimizing path histories and assemble label adjacencies through districts and junctions. -> Disjoint regions retaining large list chromatic number
- **recursion** [claim](#stmt-thm-recursive-woven) / [proof](#proof-stmt-thm-recursive-woven): Partition labels into blocks and join recursive district models with preserved terminal roles. -> Woven graph
- **main** [claim](#stmt-thm-main) / [proof](#proof-stmt-thm-recursive-woven-2): Apply recursive wovenness to an extracted region and contradict minor exclusion. -> Uniform linear list-chromatic bound

<a id="pm-s4"></a>
## 4. Engineering Triptych

### Panel 1 - epistemic contract

- **I-packing**: Under the vertex-separator hypothesis, a packing with distinct source and target ends exists and may avoid all other terminals internally.
- **I-list-bound**: List chromatic number is bounded linearly by clique-minor order with an absolute integer coefficient.

### Panel 2 - negative knowledge

- **AU-pairing**: Use free-terminal path packing to guarantee a prescribed pairing of sources and targets. -> The supplied paths can match the terminal sets in a different pairing.
- **AU-universal-algorithm**: Treat the linear list bound as a practical coloring implementation or a numerical runtime guarantee. -> The universal inequality alone does not supply a coloring program or a runtime bound.

### Panel 3 - reference implementation and oracle

Applicability: `constructive`. The vertex path-packing lemma gives a finite integral augmenting-path construction. This implementation covers that construction and does not compute the universal list-coloring constant or certify the full list-coloring theorem.

```python
# INPUTS: JSON array of {n, edges, A, B, j} finite graph instances.
# PRECONDITIONS: Simple undirected graph on range(n); disjoint terminal sets; positive integer j.
# OUTPUTS: JSON array with value=min(j, maximum packing size) and explicit paths.
# TIME: O(j*n**2) per instance using dense residual scans and unit augmentations.
# SPACE: O(n**2) per instance plus input and output storage.
# ARITHMETIC: Exact python-flint fmpz capacities and integral unit flows.
# FAILURE: Invalid input raises an exception; insufficient packing returns value below j.
import json
import sys
from collections import deque
from flint import fmpz

def pack(c):
    n, j = c['n'], c['j']
    A, B = set(c['A']), set(c['B'])
    assert type(n) is int and n >= 0 and type(j) is int and j >= 1
    assert not A & B and A | B <= set(range(n))
    arcs = set()
    for u, v in c['edges']:
        assert type(u) is int and type(v) is int and 0 <= u < n and 0 <= v < n and u != v
        edge = tuple(sorted((u,v)))
        assert edge not in arcs
        arcs.add(edge)
    s, z, size = 2*n, 2*n+1, 2*n+2
    cap = [[fmpz(0) for _ in range(size)] for _ in range(size)]
    for v in range(n):
        cap[2*v][2*v+1] = fmpz(1)
    for u, v in arcs:
        cap[2*u+1][2*v] = fmpz(j)
        cap[2*v+1][2*u] = fmpz(j)
    for a in A:
        cap[s][2*a] = fmpz(j)
    for b in B:
        cap[2*b+1][z] = fmpz(j)
    res = [row[:] for row in cap]
    def route(matrix):
        prev = {s: None}
        queue = deque([s])
        while queue and z not in prev:
            u = queue.popleft()
            for v in range(size):
                if matrix[u][v] > 0 and v not in prev:
                    prev[v] = u
                    queue.append(v)
        if z not in prev:
            return None
        path, v = [], z
        while v is not None:
            path.append(v)
            v = prev[v]
        return path[::-1]
    value = 0
    while value < j:
        path = route(res)
        if path is None:
            break
        for u, v in zip(path, path[1:]):
            res[u][v] -= 1
            res[v][u] += 1
        value += 1
    flow = [[max(fmpz(0), cap[u][v]-res[u][v]) for v in range(size)] for u in range(size)]
    paths = []
    for _ in range(value):
        walk = route(flow)
        assert walk is not None
        for u, v in zip(walk, walk[1:]):
            flow[u][v] -= 1
        p = [v//2 for v in walk if v < 2*n and v % 2 == 0]
        end = next(i for i, v in enumerate(p) if v in B)
        start = max(i for i in range(end) if p[i] in A)
        paths.append(p[start:end+1])
    return {'value': value, 'paths': paths}

print(json.dumps([pack(c) for c in json.load(sys.stdin)]))
```

OUTPUTS: JSON array with value=min(j, maximum packing size) and explicit paths.\n# TIME: O(j*n**2) per instance using dense residual scans and unit augmentations.\n# SPACE: O(n**2) per instance plus input and output storage.\n# ARITHMETIC: Exact python-flint fmpz capacities and integral unit flows.\n# FAILURE: Invalid input raises an exception; insufficient packing returns value below j.\nimport json\nimport sys\nfrom collections import deque\nfrom flint import fmpz\n\ndef pack(c):\n    n, j = c['n'], c['j']\n    A, B = set(c['A']), set(c['B'])\n    assert type(n) is int and n >= 0 and type(j) is int and j >= 1\n    assert not A & B and A | B <= set(range(n))\n    arcs = set()\n    for u, v in c['edges']:\n        assert type(u) is int and type(v) is int and 0 <= u < n and 0 <= v < n and u != v\n        edge = tuple(sorted((u,v)))\n        assert edge not in arcs\n        arcs.add(edge)\n    s, z, size = 2*n, 2*n+1, 2*n+2\n    cap = [[fmpz(0) for _ in range(size)] for _ in range(size)]\n    for v in range(n):\n        cap[2*v][2*v+1] = fmpz(1)\n    for u, v in arcs:\n        cap[2*u+1][2*v] = fmpz(j)\n        cap[2*v+1][2*u] = fmpz(j)\n    for a in A:\n        cap[s][2*a] = fmpz(j)\n    for b in B:\n        cap[2*b+1][z] = fmpz(j)\n    res = [row[:] for row in cap]\n    def route(matrix):\n        prev = {s: None}\n        queue = deque([s])\n        while queue and z not in prev:\n            u = queue.popleft()\n            for v in range(size):\n                if matrix[u][v] > 0 and v not in prev:\n                    prev[v] = u\n                    queue.append(v)\n        if z not in prev:\n            return None\n        path, v = [], z\n        while v is not None:\n            path.append(v)\n            v = prev[v]\n        return path[::-1]\n    value = 0\n    while value < j:\n        path = route(res)\n        if path is None:\n            break\n        for u, v in zip(path, path[1:]):\n            res[u][v] -= 1\n            res[v][u] += 1\n        value += 1\n    flow = [[max(fmpz(0), cap[u][v]-res[u][v]) for v in range(size)] for u in range(size)]\n    paths = []\n    for _ in range(value):\n        walk = route(flow)\n        assert walk is not None\n        for u, v in zip(walk, walk[1:]):\n            flow[u][v] -= 1\n        p = [v//2 for v in walk if v < 2*n and v % 2 == 0]\n        end = next(i for i, v in enumerate(p) if v in B)\n        start = max(i for i in range(end) if p[i] in A)\n        paths.append(p[start:end+1])\n    return {'value': value, 'paths': paths}\n\nprint(json.dumps([pack(c) for c in json.load(sys.stdin)]))\n",

<a id="pm-s5"></a>
## 5. Domain engineering contracts

| domain | applies | strength | maturity | basis | why |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| software | True | weak | adaptable | inferred | Conditional only: a software assignment problem can inherit the list-coloring existence guarantee after its conflicts and allowable assignments are faithfully represented by the graph and lists. A concrete software reduction is ABSENT from the paper. |
| games_simulation | False | none | not_applicable | inferred | A game-state representation, simulation dynamics, and a reduction of their constraints to list coloring are ABSENT. The graph-coloring theorem alone does not supply these interfaces. |
| tools | True | moderate | adaptable | inferred | A graph certificate checker can adapt the explicit definitions of list coloring and clique-model bags. This checks a submitted witness; it does not construct a coloring from the universal bound or certify an upper bound on the clique-minor order. |
| algorithms | True | strong | implementable | inferred | Vertex path packing has a finite constructive procedure: integral residual-flow augmentation on a vertex-split graph yields disjoint paths, or a separating vertex set when the required packing is infeasible. Its endpoint pairing is free. |
| data_structures | False | none | not_applicable | inferred | The paper specifies graph sets, lists, paths, and model bags but no storage layout or data-structure performance contract. A dedicated data-structure contribution is ABSENT. |
| hardware_accelerators | False | none | not_applicable | inferred | Accelerator execution, memory movement, and circuit resource constraints are ABSENT. Abstract graph density and disjoint paths do not establish a hardware mapping. |
| crypto_security | False | none | not_applicable | inferred | Cryptographic primitives, adversarial models, and security reductions are ABSENT. The probability estimates concern stable-set sampling and graph construction. |
| machine_learning | False | none | not_applicable | inferred | Training objectives, statistical generalization, and learned graph representations are ABSENT. Fractional coloring weights cover graph vertices and are not a learning guarantee. |
| optimisation_operations_research | True | weak | adaptable | inferred | Conditional feasibility application: an assignment or scheduling instance represented faithfully by a finite simple conflict graph and finite allowable lists inherits the existence guarantee. The paper supplies no scheduling reduction, cost objective, or optimized numerical coefficient. |
| distributed_systems | False | none | not_applicable | inferred | Process behavior, message schedules, failures, and a distributed execution protocol are ABSENT. Abstract connectivity and grouping of terminals do not establish agreement or liveness. |
| other (Extremal graph theory) | True | strong | inspirational | stated | In extremal graph theory, the universal linear list-coloring bound and the woven-model framework connect coloring, clique minors, and highly connected subgraphs. This is the mathematical setting explicitly treated by the paper. |

<a id="pm-s6"></a>
## 6. Applicability limits and search

- **graph-scope** (hypothesis): The graph model must be finite, simple, and undirected. An engineering interpretation requires an explicit reduction preserving conflicts and allowable assignments. Blocked use: ['Applying the bound directly to directed, infinite, or weighted assignment problems without a justified reduction.']
- **lists** (hypothesis): The conclusion concerns proper coloring from arbitrary finite vertex lists; the availability of a color at one vertex does not make it available at another. Blocked use: ['Replacing vertex lists by a shared palette without preserving local availability.']
- **constants** (unknown): The universal coefficient is expressed through absolute constants whose numerical values are not supplied. The constants are not optimized. Blocked use: ['Claiming an optimized numerical assignment budget or a practical approximation ratio from the universal theorem.']
- **existence-cost** (nonconstructive): The universal list-coloring conclusion is an existence bound. It does not itself supply a running-time or memory bound for finding a coloring or a clique minor. Blocked use: ['Treating the universal inequality as an efficient coloring algorithm or an engineering resource guarantee.']
- **small-cutoff** (hypothesis): The small-graph list bound requires minor exclusion, an order bound, and a sufficiently large integer parameter; its cutoff must be retained. Blocked use: ['Applying the small-graph proposition to arbitrary orders or to parameters below an unspecified cutoff.']
- **null-graph** (edge_case): The main theorem is stated for nonempty graphs. The null graph has a separate convention and must not be used to form a ratio with its clique-minor order. Blocked use: ['Dividing by the clique-minor order of the null graph.']
- **packing-contract** (hypothesis): Vertex path packing requires disjoint endpoint sets and survival of an endpoint-to-endpoint path after every deletion below the prescribed size. Targets are free within their endpoint set. Blocked use: ['Inferring paths for a prescribed source-target pairing, edge capacities, or packet throughput from the vertex packing statement.']
- **unpaired-minimization** (hypothesis): The sparsity conclusions for minimizing path systems rely on free endpoint assignments and minimization in the same graph where shortcut edges are tested. Blocked use: ['Applying the degeneracy or external-neighbor bounds to a fixed pairing or to a rerouted system that no longer minimizes total length.']
- **woven-endpoints** (hypothesis): Different prescribed pairs must have disjoint endpoint sets; coincidence within a pair and intersections at designated roots follow the stated conventions. Blocked use: ['Using wovenness for arbitrary overlapping pairs or allowing arbitrary intersections between the model and the paths.']
- **fractional-transfer** (approximation): A fractional coloring supply does not directly yield a linear list coloring. Eligibility and the global assignment of colors to bins are essential parts of the transfer. Blocked use: ['Replacing the list-coloring proof by unrestricted repeated stable-set sampling.']
- **universal-base** (edge_case): The universal conclusion covers the finite base range; the sufficiently-large restrictions in intermediate lemmas are not small-parameter exceptions to the final bound. Blocked use: ['Presenting the final theorem as only asymptotic in the clique-minor order.']

<a id="pm-formal"></a>
### Formal statement (Lean 4)

Corpus status: formalized in the source corpus (toolchain `leanprover/lean4:v4.34.1`, Mathlib `d13f23b723b8a846827a245b89c10fc7d3f11612`). Not re-checked here; the statements give the exact quantifiers and hypotheses, not a proof.

Scope note of family 157 (`lean/docs/157.md`, verbatim):

> The following describes the scope of the Lean formalization related to the following accompanying paper(s):
>
> - [A linear list-coloring bound in terms of the Hadwiger number](../../preprints/A-linear-list-coloring-bound-in-terms-of-the-Hadwiger-number-September-23-2026/paper.pdf)
> - [A counterexample to Hadwiger's conjecture](../../preprints/A-counterexample-to-Hadwigers-conjecture-September-23-2026/paper.pdf)
>
> ## Scope
>
> Hadwiger's conjecture predicts $\chi(G)\le h(G)$ for every finite graph, where $h(G)$ is the largest clique-minor order. The formalization constructs arbitrarily large finite simple counterexamples with independence number at most two. For a graph on $m$ vertices it proves
> $h(G)<26m/75+2/3<m/2\le\chi(G)$.
> This disproves the ordinary chromatic form. The paper's fractional-chromatic strengthening and the Colin de Verdière consequence are outside this selected statement.
>
> The Linear List Hadwiger conjecture asks for a universal linear bound on list chromatic number in terms of clique-minor size. The formalization proves that there is one integer $C\ge1$ such that every finite nonempty simple graph $G$ satisfies $\chi_{\mathrm{list}}(G)\le C h(G)$, where $h(G)$ is the largest order of a clique minor. The constant is independent of the graph.

```lean
import Mathlib

namespace OAI

namespace LinearListHadwiger

def ListColorable {V : Type} (G : SimpleGraph V) {Color : Type}
    (L : V → Finset Color) : Prop :=
  ∃ c : V → Color, (∀ v, c v ∈ L v) ∧ ∀ ⦃v w⦄, G.Adj v w → c v ≠ c w

def Choosable {V : Type} (G : SimpleGraph V) (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ (Color : Type) (L : V → Finset Color), (∀ v, k ≤ (L v).card) → ListColorable G L

noncomputable def listChromaticNumber {V : Type} (G : SimpleGraph V) : ℕ :=
  sInf {k : ℕ | Choosable G k}

def HasCliqueMinor {V : Type} (G : SimpleGraph V) (t : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ B : Fin t → Set V,
    (∀ i, (G.induce (B i)).Connected) ∧
    (∀ i j, i ≠ j → Disjoint (B i) (B j)) ∧
    (∀ i j, i ≠ j → ∃ v ∈ B i, ∃ w ∈ B j, G.Adj v w)

noncomputable def hadwigerNumber {V : Type} (G : SimpleGraph V) : ℕ :=
  sSup {t : ℕ | HasCliqueMinor G t}

def MainStatement : Prop :=
  ∃ C : ℕ, 1 ≤ C ∧ ∀ (V : Type) [Fintype V] [Nonempty V] (G : SimpleGraph V),
    listChromaticNumber G ≤ C * hadwigerNumber G

theorem main_theorem : MainStatement := by
  sorry

end LinearListHadwiger

end OAI
```

<a id="pm-s7"></a>
## 7. Complete mathematical paper


We prove that every finite nonempty graph <i>G</i> satisfies $`\chi_{\mathrm{list}}(G)\le C h(G)`$ for an absolute integer <i>C</i>, where $`h(G)`$ is the largest order of a clique minor. This resolves the Linear List Hadwiger conjecture affirmatively.

<a id="sec:introduction"></a>
### Introduction

A clique minor records a form of complete interaction inside a graph: its vertices are represented by disjoint connected sets, and every two sets have an edge between them. For a finite nonempty simple graph $G$, let $h(G)$ be the largest order of a clique minor in $G$. Hadwiger conjectured that the chromatic number always satisfies $\chi(G)\le h(G)$ (Hadwiger 1943) <a id="pm-cite-1"></a>[[Hadwiger1943](#ref-Hadwiger1943)]. The companion manuscript (OpenAI 2026, Corollary 1.2) <a id="pm-cite-2"></a>[[OpenAIHadwigerCounterexample2026](#ref-OpenAIHadwigerCounterexample2026)] constructs finite simple graphs with $\chi(G)>h(G)$, disproving this ordinary coefficient-one assertion. Its linear relaxation asks whether an absolute constant can replace the coefficient one. We prove a bound of this form even when allowable colors vary from vertex to vertex.

A *list assignment* $\mathcal L$ assigns a finite set of colors to each vertex. An $\mathcal L$-coloring is a proper coloring $c$ satisfying $c(v)\in\mathcal L(v)$ at every vertex. The list chromatic number $\ell(G)=\chi_{\mathrm{list}}(G)$ is the least integer $k$ for which every assignment with $|\mathcal L(v)|\ge k$ is colorable. List coloring was introduced independently by Vizing (Vizing 1976) <a id="pm-cite-3"></a>[[Vizing1976](#ref-Vizing1976)] and by Erdős, Rubin, and Taylor (Erdős, Rubin, and Taylor 1980) <a id="pm-cite-4"></a>[[ErdosRubinTaylor1980](#ref-ErdosRubinTaylor1980)]. The linear list version of Hadwiger’s conjecture was formulated by Kawarabayashi and Mohar (Kawarabayashi and Mohar 2007, Conjecture 1.3) <a id="pm-cite-5"></a>[[KawarabayashiMohar2007](#ref-KawarabayashiMohar2007)].

<a id="stmt-thm-main"></a>
<div id="thm:main" class="theorem">

**Theorem 1**. *There is an absolute integer $C\ge1$ such that every finite nonempty simple graph $G$ satisfies $$\ell(G)\le C h(G).$$*

</div>

Thus the Linear List Hadwiger conjecture has an affirmative resolution. The constant is independent of the graph order, the list assignment, and the number of distinct colors appearing in its union. Taking the same list at every vertex immediately gives the ordinary conclusion.

<a id="stmt-cor-ordinary"></a>
<div id="cor:ordinary" class="corollary">

**Corollary 2**. *Every finite nonempty simple graph $G$ satisfies $\chi(G)\le C h(G)$, with the constant $C$ in Theorem <a href="#thm:main" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:main">1</a>.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-cor-ordinary"><summary>Proof of stmt-cor-ordinary</summary>

*Proof.* A coloring from the common list $\{1,\ldots,\ell(G)\}$ shows that $\chi(G)\le\ell(G)$. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-3"></a>
#### Prior work and the two obstacles

The density theorems of Kostochka (Kostochka 1982, 1984) <a id="pm-cite-6"></a>[[Kostochka1982](#ref-Kostochka1982), [Kostochka1984](#ref-Kostochka1984)] and Thomason (Thomason 1984) <a id="pm-cite-7"></a>[[Thomason1984](#ref-Thomason1984)] show that every $K_t$-minor-free graph has a vertex of degree $O(t\sqrt{\log t})$, as does each of its subgraphs. Greedy coloring in reverse deletion order therefore gives this bound for arbitrary lists. Norin, Postle, and Song (Norin, Postle, and Song 2023) <a id="pm-cite-8"></a>[[NorinPostleSong2023](#ref-NorinPostleSong2023)] went beyond that degeneracy threshold for ordinary coloring, proving $O(t(\log t)^\beta)$ for every fixed $\beta>1/4$. Norin and Postle (Norin and Postle 2023) <a id="pm-cite-9"></a>[[NorinPostle2023](#ref-NorinPostle2023)] extended such bounds to list coloring using the structure of highly connected minor-free graphs.

The coefficient in a linear list bound has a different role from the coefficient in ordinary Hadwiger’s conjecture. Voigt (Voigt 1993) <a id="pm-cite-10"></a>[[Voigt1993](#ref-Voigt1993)] constructed planar graphs that are not $4$-choosable. Barát, Joret, and Wood (Barát, Joret, and Wood 2011) <a id="pm-cite-11"></a>[[BaratJoretWood2011](#ref-BaratJoretWood2011)] constructed graphs with no $K_{3s+2}$ minor that are not $4s$-choosable for every integer $s\ge1$, and Steiner (Steiner 2022) <a id="pm-cite-12"></a>[[Steiner2022List](#ref-Steiner2022List)] proved that for every $\varepsilon>0$ and all sufficiently large $t$ there are $K_t$-minor-free graphs with list chromatic number at least $(2-\varepsilon)t$. Thus a universal constant in Theorem <a href="#thm:main" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:main">1</a> must be at least two. Our constants are not optimized.

The fractional coloring theorem of Reed and Seymour (Reed and Seymour 1998) <a id="pm-cite-13"></a>[[ReedSeymour1998](#ref-ReedSeymour1998)] gives $\chi_f(G)\le2h(G)$, where fractional coloring permits weighted stable sets in place of color classes. It provides a linear supply of stable sets but does not directly give a linear ordinary or list coloring: naive repeated sampling introduces a factor depending on the graph order. Delcourt and Postle (Delcourt and Postle 2025) <a id="pm-cite-14"></a>[[DelcourtPostle2021](#ref-DelcourtPostle2021)] obtained the ordinary bound $O(t\log\log t)$ for graphs excluding a $K_t$ minor and reduced a linear ordinary bound to coloring suitably small subgraphs. Liu and Luo (Liu and Luo 2026) <a id="pm-cite-15"></a>[[LiuLuo2026](#ref-LiuLuo2026)] subsequently proved the ordinary bound $O(t\log\log\log t)$ and developed bounded stable-set sampling that we use below.[^1] These ordinary-coloring statements do not by themselves give colorings from arbitrary vertex lists.

For list coloring, Postle proved an $O(t(\log\log t)^6)$ bound for $K_t$-minor-free graphs (Postle 2020, Theorem 1.8) <a id="pm-cite-16"></a>[[Postle2020](#ref-Postle2020)]. His separability and woven-minor constructions provide the structural framework for our passage from small graphs to arbitrary orders. Delcourt and Postle outlined an $O(t(\log\log t)^2)$ list bound in the first version of their paper (Delcourt and Postle 2021, sec. 6) <a id="pm-cite-17"></a>[[DelcourtPostle2021v1](#ref-DelcourtPostle2021v1)], leaving the details to the reader. In subsequent work posted on October 1, 2026, Gu and Xu (Gu and Xu 2026, Theorem 1.3) <a id="pm-cite-18"></a>[[GuXu2026](#ref-GuXu2026)] proved an $O(t\log\log t)$ list bound. Connectivity extraction by the constraint-budget method of Girão and Narayanan (Girão and Narayanan 2022) <a id="pm-cite-19"></a>[[GiraoNarayanan2022](#ref-GiraoNarayanan2022)], and the highly linked graph theorem of Bollobás and Thomason (Bollobás and Thomason 1996) <a id="pm-cite-20"></a>[[BollobasThomason1996](#ref-BollobasThomason1996)], are further key antecedents. We reproduce the list transfer, density, path accounting, and recursion arguments in the forms required here.

Two difficulties remain after these reductions. Even on a small graph, a sampled stable set cannot be given a single color unless that color is available at every vertex receiving it. In a graph of unrestricted order, the paths used to assemble a minor may themselves contain arbitrarily many vertices. Their deletion must therefore be charged through their structure, rather than through their order. The proof addresses these two difficulties separately.

<a id="pm-h-4"></a>
#### Proof strategy

First, Proposition <a href="#prop:small-list" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:small-list">9</a> proves that a $K_t$-minor-free graph on at most $t^{11/10}$ vertices is $Lt$-choosable, for an absolute $L$ and all sufficiently large $t$. We partition the union of all lists into bins, assigning each color to a single bin throughout the graph. A vertex is eligible for a bin precisely when its own list contains a color in that bin. A random partition gives every vertex enough eligible bins at every stage, before any remaining graph is chosen. Lemma <a href="#small:eligible-thinning" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="small:eligible-thinning">10</a> then repeatedly halves an upper bound on the fractional chromatic number using sampled stable sets restricted to eligible vertices. Vertices assigned to the same bin lie in one stable set, so each can choose its own allowable color from that bin; colors in different bins cannot conflict.

To prove the thinning lemma, suppose every sampling outcome leaves a fractional chromatic number greater than half the current bound. A deterministic separator decomposition finds a fixed highly connected subgraph in which a remainder still has large expected fractional chromatic number. Independent repetitions produce disjoint private vertex sets, each supporting a clique model. A small, fixed family of matching tests shows that the complement of the union of the sampled remainders remains highly connected. Connecting equally labeled bags through this complement produces the excluded clique minor. The proof uses bounded stable-set sampling and ordinary-chromatic connectivity extraction, with the full argument given in Section <a href="#small:section" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="small:section">3</a>. Summing the costs of successive halving stages requires only $O(t)$ bins.

Second, Lemma <a href="#lem:list-extraction" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:list-extraction">17</a> extracts highly connected subgraphs with a linear loss of list chromatic number. The additive list-deletion estimate, Lemma <a href="#lem:additive-deletion" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:additive-deletion">19</a>, reserves colors for a small set and controls its interaction with all remaining vertices. Its probabilistic estimate tests only polynomially many exceptional vertices, independently of the ambient graph order and palette size. Minimum-length path systems give the sparsity needed to apply this estimate even when the paths are long. The density argument also supplies small highly connected subgraphs in which clique models can be built while connecting paths are rerouted.

The sequential construction in Lemma <a href="#lem:separability" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:separability">34</a> then shows that a graph of sufficiently large list chromatic number either contains the desired clique minor or splits into two disjoint subgraphs retaining nearly all of that list chromatic number. At each step, one small district supplies new adjacencies between model bags and a separate junction joins the paths carrying those bags forward. The deletion estimate applies to the complete history of original minimizing paths, including vertices no longer used by the growing model.

Finally, Theorem <a href="#thm:recursive-woven" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:recursive-woven">36</a> builds a clique model whose bags contain prescribed roots, together with paths for prescribed terminal pairs. After reserving the paths for the terminal pairs, the remaining task is a rooted model inside a fresh region. Separability supplies three disjoint districts for recursive calls. Partitioning the root labels into three blocks and assigning one district to each pair of blocks reduces each call to about two thirds as many roots, while every pair of labels still occurs together in one district. Connectivity extraction and the case with no prescribed pairs complete the theorem.

Section <a href="#sec:preliminaries" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:preliminaries">2</a> fixes the external inputs and probabilistic tools. Section <a href="#small:section" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="small:section">3</a> proves the small-graph list bound, and Section <a href="#sec:list-transfer" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:list-transfer">4</a> establishes list extraction and deletion. Section <a href="#sec:density" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:density">5</a> constructs small highly connected districts; Section <a href="#sec:routing" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:routing">6</a> develops their routing interfaces. Sections <a href="#sec:separability" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:separability">7</a> and <a href="#sec:recursion" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:recursion">8</a> prove separability and the final recursive theorem. The only structural results used without proof are the fractional minor bound, ordinary-chromatic connectivity extraction, and the terminal grouping theorem, whose precise statements follow.

<a id="sec:preliminaries"></a>
### Preliminaries and probabilistic tools

All graphs are finite, simple, and undirected. A *stable set* is a set of pairwise nonadjacent vertices. For a vertex set $X$, write $P[X]$ for the induced subgraph and $P-X=P[V(P)\setminus X]$. A clique model consists of disjoint nonempty connected vertex sets, called *bags*, with an edge between every two bags. Models lift through edge contractions and vertex deletions, so $h$ is nonincreasing under taking minors. Whenever a subgraph is specified by its vertices, it is induced. Adding edges to a connected or highly connected subgraph preserves the corresponding property, so the subgraphs produced below may be replaced by induced subgraphs on their vertices.

A graph is $k$-connected if it has more than $k$ vertices and remains connected after deletion of fewer than $k$ vertices. Such a graph has minimum degree at least $k$. A separator split is a partition $V(P)=A\mathbin{\dot\cup}Z\mathbin{\dot\cup}A'$, with $A,A'$ nonempty and anticomplete. If $|V(P)|>k$ and $P$ is not $k$-connected, there is such a split with $|Z|<k$. Deleting $z<k$ vertices from a $k$-connected graph leaves a $(k-z)$-connected graph. All logarithms are natural. The null graph has $h=\ell=\chi=f=0$. Integer parameters include minor orders, connectivity requirements, and numbers of paths; powers bounding graph orders need not be integers.

<a id="pm-h-6"></a>
#### Fractional coloring and established structural results

The fractional chromatic number $f(P)$ is the minimum total weight of nonnegative weights on the stable sets of $P$ that cover every vertex with weight at least one. Finite linear-programming duality (Gale, Kuhn, and Tucker 1951) <a id="pm-cite-21"></a>[[galekuhntucker1951](#ref-galekuhntucker1951)] gives <a id="eq:fractional-dual"></a>$$\label{eq:fractional-dual}
 f(P)=\max\left\{\sum_{v\in V(P)}w(v):
 w(v)\ge0,\quad \sum_{v\in I}w(v)\le1
 \text{ for every stable set }I\right\}.$$ The primal is feasible, using singleton stable sets, and has a finite optimum; thus this use of duality has no feasibility or boundedness exception. For $r>0$, $f(P)\le r$ is equivalent to a distribution on stable sets with every vertex included with probability at least $1/r$. Indeed, divide a fractional coloring by $r$ and put any missing mass on the empty set; conversely multiply such a distribution by $r$. Restriction to an induced subgraph cannot increase $f$, and adding one vertex increases it by at most one.

<a id="stmt-thm-fractional"></a>
<div id="thm:fractional" class="theorem">

**Theorem 3** (Fractional minor bound). *Every graph $P$ satisfies $f(P)\le4h(P)$.*

</div>

This follows from the stronger bound $f(P)\le2h(P)$ of Reed and Seymour (Reed and Seymour 1998, Statement (1.3)) <a id="pm-cite-22"></a>[[ReedSeymour1998](#ref-ReedSeymour1998)]. We keep the factor four throughout.

<a id="stmt-thm-ordinary-extraction"></a>
<div id="thm:ordinary-extraction" class="theorem">

**Theorem 4** (Ordinary-chromatic connectivity extraction). *If $k\ge1$ is an integer and $\chi(P)\ge7k$, then $P$ has a $k$-connected subgraph $J$ with $\chi(J)\ge\chi(P)-6k$.*

</div>

We use the form stated in (Delcourt and Postle 2025, Theorem 5.1) <a id="pm-cite-23"></a>[[DelcourtPostle2021](#ref-DelcourtPostle2021)], attributed there to Girão and Narayanan. There is no minor-exclusion hypothesis. In particular the theorem applies to auxiliary clique blow-ups, which need not inherit any minor exclusion.

<a id="stmt-thm-grouping"></a>
<div id="thm:grouping" class="theorem">

**Theorem 5** (Grouping terminals). *There is an absolute integer $\gamma\ge1$ such that the following holds. In a $\gamma m$-connected graph, every partition of $m\ge1$ distinct terminals into nonempty groups can be realized by pairwise disjoint connected vertex sets, one containing each group.*

</div>

This is a consequence of the highly linked graph theorem of Bollobás and Thomason (Bollobás and Thomason 1996) <a id="pm-cite-24"></a>[[BollobasThomason1996](#ref-BollobasThomason1996)]; we use the case with second knitting parameter one in (Delcourt and Postle 2025, Definition 5.7 and Theorem 5.8) <a id="pm-cite-25"></a>[[DelcourtPostle2021](#ref-DelcourtPostle2021)]. The constant $\gamma$ is uniform in the number and sizes of the groups. For a group of size two, a path within its connected set joins its terminals. We will apply this observation to any prescribed pairing of distinct terminals.

<a id="pm-h-7"></a>
#### Bounded sampling and concentration

The following real-parameter form of bounded stable-set sampling is convenient. Its integer-parameter form appears in (Liu and Luo 2026, Lemma 4.1) <a id="pm-cite-26"></a>[[LiuLuo2026](#ref-LiuLuo2026)]; we include the short proof.

<a id="stmt-lem-bounded"></a>
<div id="lem:bounded" class="lemma">

**Lemma 6**. *Suppose $|V(P)|\le n$, where $n\ge1$, and $f(P)\le r$, where $r\ge1$. There is a distribution on stable sets $I$ such that $$|I|\le\lceil n/r\rceil,
 \qquad \Pr(v\in I)=\frac1{2r}\quad(v\in V(P)).$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-bounded"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-bounded</summary>

*Proof.* Start with a stable-set distribution having inclusion probabilities at least $1/r$. Conditional independent deletion of each included vertex reduces every marginal to exactly $1/r$ and preserves stability. Put $M=\lceil n/r\rceil$. Partition each resulting stable set $I$ into parts of size at most $M$, assigning its probability mass to each part. This gives a finite measure of total mass at most $$\mathbb E\bigl(1+|I|/M\bigr)
 =1+|V(P)|/(rM)\le2.$$ Every vertex still has mass $1/r$. Add mass on the empty set to make the total exactly two and divide by two. ◻

</details>

We also record the standard bounded-martingale-difference estimate (Azuma 1967; McDiarmid 1989) <a id="pm-cite-27"></a>[[azuma1967](#ref-azuma1967), [mcdiarmid1989](#ref-mcdiarmid1989)], with its short exponential-moment proof.

<a id="stmt-lem-concentration"></a>
<div id="lem:concentration" class="lemma">

**Lemma 7** (Bounded differences). *Let $Z$ be a function of $s\ge1$ independent finite random variables. If changing one variable changes $Z$ by at most $b>0$, then $$\Pr\bigl(|Z-\mathbb EZ|\ge u\bigr)
 \le2\exp\bigl(-u^2/(2sb^2)\bigr)\qquad(u>0).$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-concentration"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-concentration</summary>

*Proof.* Expose the variables in order. The martingale of conditional expectations has differences of conditional mean zero and absolute value at most $b$. Convexity bounds the conditional exponential moment of a difference at $\lambda$ by $\cosh(\lambda b)\le\exp(\lambda^2b^2/2)$. Multiplying these bounds and applying Markov’s inequality with $\lambda=u/(sb^2)$ gives the upper tail. Apply the same argument to $-Z$ and add the two bounds. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-8"></a>
#### A small family of connectivity tests

The next test replaces an enumeration of arbitrary vertex cuts by an enumeration of unions of a few open neighborhoods. The family is fixed before the random deleted set is chosen.

<a id="stmt-lem-cut-test"></a>
<div id="lem:cut-test" class="lemma">

**Lemma 8** (Cut test). *Let $P$ be a $k$-connected graph on at most $n$ vertices, where $k$ is a sufficiently large integer. Set $$s=\left\lceil10(n/k)\log(2n)\right\rceil.$$ There is a family of at most $(n+1)^{s+1}$ matchings, each of size $\lfloor k/8\rfloor$, with the following property. If $U\subseteq V(P)$, every vertex of $P$ has at least $k/2$ neighbors outside $U$, and fewer than $k/32$ endpoints of each matching belong to $U$, then $P-U$ is $\lfloor k/32\rfloor$-connected.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-cut-test"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-cut-test</summary>

*Proof.* For every set $R$ of at most $s$ vertices, put $B_R=\bigcup_{v\in R}N_P(v)$. Whenever both $B_R$ and its complement have size at least $k/3$, fix a matching of size $\lfloor k/8\rfloor$ across this cut. Such a matching exists: otherwise the endpoints of a maximal smaller matching form a vertex cover of the crossing edges, of size less than $k/4$. Both sides remain nonempty after their removal, contradicting $k$-connectivity. The number of possible sets $R$, and hence of matchings, is at most $(n+1)^{s+1}$.

The neighborhood assumption ensures that $P-U$ has more than $\lfloor k/32\rfloor$ vertices. If it fails the asserted connectivity, there are a set $Z\subseteq V(P)\setminus U$ with $|Z|<k/32$ and nonempty anticomplete sides $A,A'$ partitioning $V(P)\setminus(U\cup Z)$. Every vertex of either side has more than $k/3$ neighbors in that same side, since it has at least $k/2$ neighbors outside $U$ and loses fewer than $k/32$ to $Z$. In particular both sides have size at least $k/3$.

Make $s$ independent uniform draws from $A$. For each vertex $v\in A$, the probability that none of the draws is an open neighbor of $v$ is at most $\exp(-ks/(3n))$. The union bound over $A$ is less than one by the choice of $s$. Thus the set $R$ of drawn vertices, after repetitions are removed, satisfies $A\subseteq B_R$. Since $A,A'$ are anticomplete, $A'\cap B_R=\varnothing$. The matching fixed for this cut has every edge incident with $U\cup Z$, for otherwise an edge would join $A$ to $A'$. But $U$ contains fewer than $k/32$ of its endpoints, and $Z$ contains fewer than $k/32$ vertices. They cannot cover its $\lfloor k/8\rfloor$ disjoint edges. This contradiction proves the lemma. ◻

</details>

<a id="small:section"></a>
### List coloring small graphs

<a id="stmt-prop-small-list"></a>
<div id="prop:small-list" class="proposition">

**Proposition 9**. *There are an absolute positive integer $L$ and an absolute integer $t_0$ such that, for every integer $t\ge t_0$ and every graph $G$, $$h(G)<t,\qquad |V(G)|\le t^{11/10}
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \ell(G)\le Lt.$$*

</div>

We will color the graph in stages, halving an upper bound on its fractional chromatic number at each stage. For each sampled stable set, only a specified subset of vertices is eligible to be removed. The next lemma allows these eligibility restrictions to be fixed in advance. In the final application they will come from one partition of the actual colors appearing in the lists, chosen before the successive remaining graphs are determined.

<a id="stmt-small-eligible-thinning"></a>
<div id="small:eligible-thinning" class="lemma">

**Lemma 10** (Eligible thinning). *There is an absolute positive integer $B$ such that the following holds for all sufficiently large integers $t$. Let $n,r$ be real parameters with $$1\le n\le t^{11/10},\qquad \frac{t}{\log t}\le r\le4t,$$ and let $P$ be a graph with $|V(P)|\le n$, $h(P)<t$, and $f(P)\le r$. Set $$N=\left\lceil Br\log\bigl(2\max\{1,t/r\}\bigr)\right\rceil.$$ Suppose $E_1,\ldots,E_N\subseteq V(P)$ contain every vertex at least $N/2$ times. There are stable sets $I_1,\ldots,I_N$ of $P$, each of size at most $\lceil n/r\rceil$, such that $$f\left(P-\bigcup_{j=1}^N(I_j\cap E_j)\right)\le r/2.$$ The cutoff for $t$ is uniform over $P,n,r$ and the eligibility sets.*

</div>

We prove the lemma by contradiction. If every sampled remainder has fractional chromatic number greater than $r/2$, we first find a fixed highly connected subgraph $H$ where a remainder still has large expected fractional chromatic number. Fresh independent remainders then contain disjoint subsets, each carrying a clique model. The complement in $H$ of the union of the remainders remains highly connected. To assemble a $K_t$ model, partition its $t$ labels into small blocks and use one of these disjoint models for each block and each pair of blocks. The complement connects all bags assigned to the same label. Every pair of labels is represented together in one model, so the resulting label sets are adjacent. The estimates below provide the models and the connectivity for this construction.

<a id="pm-h-10"></a>
#### Eligible samples and uniform concentration

<a id="small:B-choice"></a>
We prove Lemma <a href="#small:eligible-thinning" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="small:eligible-thinning">10</a> with the following fixed choice of $B$. Let $\gamma$ be the integer in Theorem <a href="#thm:grouping" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:grouping">5</a>. Fix <a id="small:constants"></a>$$\label{small:constants}
 D_0=10^6\gamma,\qquad Q_0=401^2,$$ and choose a positive integer $B$ such that $$\label{small:B-choice}
 B\ge16,\qquad
 2^{B/4}\ge
 \max\bigl\{2000(D_0+1),\,10^4Q_0^2\bigr\}.$$ These constants remain fixed throughout this section.

<a id="small:range"></a>
<a id="small:parameter-bounds"></a>
<a id="small:attachment-budget"></a>
Consider an integer $t$ and real parameters $n,r$ satisfying $$\label{small:range}
 1\le n\le t^{11/10},\qquad
 \frac{t}{\log t}\le r\le4t.$$ Let $P$ be a graph on at most $n$ vertices with $h(P)<t$ and $f(P)\le r$. Set <a id="small:parameters"></a>$$\label{small:parameters}
 \begin{gathered}
 y=\max\{1,t/r\},\qquad x=\lfloor r/200\rfloor,
 \qquad q=\lceil t/x\rceil^2,\qquad k=\lceil D_0ty\rceil,\\
 N=\lceil Br\log(2y)\rceil,\qquad M=\lceil n/r\rceil.
 \end{gathered}$$ Here $x$ bounds the size of a label block, $q$ bounds the number of disjoint clique models, and $k$ is the connectivity required of $H$. The parameters $N$ and $M$ are the number of trials and the maximum size of one sampled stable set. We always take $t$ above an absolute cutoff large enough that $r\ge400$. In particular $x\ge1$. The following bounds hold uniformly in <a href="#small:range" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="small:range">[small:range]</a>: $$\label{small:parameter-bounds}
 \begin{gathered}
 1\le y\le\log t,\qquad \frac{t}{y}\le r\le\frac{4t}{y},\qquad
 x\ge\frac r{400},\\
 q\le Q_0y^2,\qquad xq\le403ty,\qquad
 D_0ty\le k\le(D_0+1)ty.
 \end{gathered}$$ Indeed, $t/x\le400t/r\le400y$, so $\lceil t/x\rceil\le401y$. Also $$x\lceil t/x\rceil^2
 \le\frac{t^2}{x}+2t+x
 \le400\frac{t^2}{r}+2t+\frac r{200}
 \le403ty.$$ Our choice of $D_0$ consequently gives, for all sufficiently large $t$, $$\label{small:attachment-budget}
 k\ge r,\qquad 2xq<\frac{k}{64},\qquad
 \left\lfloor\frac{k}{32}\right\rfloor\ge\gamma(2xq).$$

<a id="small:remainder"></a>
<a id="small:survival"></a>
<a id="small:sparseness"></a>
Fix sets $E_1,\ldots,E_N\subseteq V(P)$ such that each vertex belongs to at least $N/2$ of them. These are the eligibility sets and are fixed before sampling. Independently for each $j\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$, sample a stable set $I_j$ from the distribution in Lemma <a href="#lem:bounded" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:bounded">6</a>, with $$|I_j|\le M,\qquad \Pr(v\in I_j)=\frac1{2r}.$$ The covered vertices at trial $j$ are $I_j\cap E_j$, and the remainder is $$\label{small:remainder}
 W=V(P)\setminus\bigcup_{j=1}^N(I_j\cap E_j).$$ For every vertex $v$, independence of the trials and the eligibility condition imply $$\label{small:survival}
 \Pr(v\in W)
 \le\left(1-\frac1{2r}\right)^{N/2}
 \le p:=\exp\left(-\frac{N}{4r}\right)
 \le(2y)^{-B/4}.$$ In particular, <a href="#small:B-choice" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="small:B-choice">[small:B-choice]</a> and <a href="#small:parameter-bounds" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="small:parameter-bounds">[small:parameter-bounds]</a> give $$\label{small:sparseness}
 2kp\le\frac r{1000},\qquad q^2p\le10^{-4}.$$ For the first inequality, divide by $r$ and use $$\frac{2kp}{r}
 \le2(D_0+1)y^2(2y)^{-B/4}
 \le2(D_0+1)2^{-B/4}.$$ For the second, use $q^2p\le Q_0^2y^4(2y)^{-B/4}\le Q_0^2 2^{-B/4}$.

<a id="stmt-small-concentration"></a>
<div id="small:concentration" class="lemma">

**Lemma 11**. *Take at most $q$ independent copies of the experiment <a href="#small:remainder" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="small:remainder">[small:remainder]</a>. Let $Z$ be any one of the following quantities, where the vertex set $A\subseteq V(P)$ is fixed before sampling: $$|A\cap W_i|,\qquad
 \left|A\cap\bigcup_iW_i\right|,\qquad
 f(P[A\cap W_i]).$$ For each fixed $\delta>0$, and all sufficiently large $t$, <a id="small:uniform-tail"></a>$$\label{small:uniform-tail}
 \Pr\bigl(|Z-\mathbb EZ|\ge\delta r\bigr)
 \le2\exp(-t^{7/10}),$$ uniformly over all the data in <a href="#small:range" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="small:range">[small:range]</a> and all eligibility sets satisfying the stated condition.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-small-concentration"><summary>Proof of stmt-small-concentration</summary>

*Proof.* Changing one sampled stable set changes $W_i$ on at most $2M$ vertices. It changes a union of remainders on at most the same number of vertices. Adding or deleting a vertex changes fractional chromatic number by at most one, so all the quantities in the statement have bounded differences at most $2M$ per trial.

For sufficiently large $t$, $r\log(2y)\ge1$, and hence $N\le(B+1)r\log(2y)$. With $A_0=4Q_0(B+1)$, we obtain $$qN\le A_0ty\log(2y),\qquad M\le2t^{1/10}y.$$ Lemma <a href="#lem:concentration" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:concentration">7</a> therefore gives $$\begin{aligned}
 \Pr\bigl(|Z-\mathbb EZ|\ge\delta r\bigr)
 &\le2\exp\left(-\frac{\delta^2r^2}{2(qN)(2M)^2}\right)\\
 &\le2\exp\left(
 -\frac{\delta^2t^{4/5}}{32A_0y^5\log(2y)}\right).
\end{aligned}$$ Since $1\le y\le\log t$, the exponent in the last line has magnitude at least $t^{7/10}$ for all sufficiently large $t$. The cutoff depends only on $\delta$ and the fixed constants. Independence between different vertices is not used. ◻

</details>

All asymptotic probability estimates below are uniform over these data. Only finitely many fixed positive values of $\delta$ will be used in Lemma <a href="#small:concentration" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="small:concentration">11</a>, so their cutoffs can be combined.

<a id="pm-h-11"></a>
#### Localizing a failure of thinning

<a id="stmt-small-fixed-region"></a>
<div id="small:fixed-region" class="lemma">

<a id="small:region-expectation"></a>
**Lemma 12**. *Suppose that every outcome of the experiment <a href="#small:remainder" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="small:remainder">[small:remainder]</a> having positive probability satisfies $f(P[W])>r/2$. Then there is a fixed induced $k$-connected subgraph $H\subseteq P$ such that $$\label{small:region-expectation}
 \mathbb E f(H[W\cap V(H)])>r/4.$$ The subgraph $H$ is chosen before any fresh copies of the experiment are sampled.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-small-fixed-region"><summary>Proof of stmt-small-fixed-region</summary>

*Proof.* Build a binary decomposition of $P$, making all choices before sampling. A node is an induced subgraph. Stop at a node of order at most $2k$, and also at a larger node which is $k$-connected. Otherwise choose a separator of size less than $k$, partition the vertices outside it into two nonempty anticomplete sides, and form two children by adding the separator to each side.

There are $O(n^2+1)$ nodes. To see this, give a node of order $u>2k$ potential $u-k$. Each large child’s potential is strictly smaller than its parent’s, since the other exclusive side is nonempty. If both children are large, their potentials sum to at most their parent’s: their orders sum to $u+|S|<u+k$, where $S$ is the separator. If just one child is large, its potential alone is at most the parent’s. Thus at each depth the sum of the large-node potentials is at most $n$, while the depth of a large-node branch is at most $n$. The small leaves contribute at most two children per large node, in addition to a possible small root.

Every separator and every small leaf has order at most $2k$. Its expected intersection size with $W$ is at most $2kp\le r/1000$. Lemma <a href="#small:concentration" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="small:concentration">11</a> and a union bound over the decomposition show that, with probability $1-o(1)$, all these intersections have fewer than $r/100$ vertices. If every $k$-connected leaf had expected fractional chromatic number at most $r/4$ after restriction to $W$, the same lemma would give, again with probability $1-o(1)$, fractional chromatic number less than $3r/10$ in every such leaf. A small leaf has this latter bound as well, since its fractional chromatic number is at most its order.

Fix an outcome satisfying all these conclusions. Write $F=P[W]$. The assumption of the lemma gives $f(F)>r/2$, whereas every leaf restriction has fractional chromatic number less than $3r/10$. We compare these bounds by replacing every vertex of $F$ with a clique of the same large order. Ordinary-chromatic connectivity extraction in this larger graph will produce a subgraph of large chromatic number that cannot cross any of the blown-up separators. It must lie in one blown-up leaf, giving the contradiction.

<a id="small:blowup-lower"></a>
For a positive integer $m$, form $F^{(m)}$ by replacing each vertex of $F$ with a clique of order $m$, and replacing each edge with a complete join between its two replacement cliques. Every color class of $F^{(m)}$ projects to a stable set of $F$ and uses at most one vertex of each replacement clique. Dividing the multiplicities of these projected stable sets by $m$ therefore gives a fractional coloring of $F$. Consequently $$\label{small:blowup-lower}
 \chi(F^{(m)})\ge mf(F)>mr/2.$$

For each leaf restriction, choose a fractional coloring of weight less than $3r/10$. Round its finitely many stable-set weights up to multiples of $1/m$. Give a distinct color slot to each unit of weight $1/m$. Every original vertex belongs to at least $m$ slots, so its $m$ copies can be assigned distinct slots containing that vertex. A slot is a stable set upstairs: it contains at most one copy of any original vertex, and its original vertices form a stable set. The rounding adds only a bounded number of slots, independent of $m$ for this fixed leaf. There are finitely many leaves, so for all sufficiently large $m$, every blown-up leaf restriction has a coloring with fewer than $31mr/100$ colors.

Apply Theorem <a href="#thm:ordinary-extraction" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:ordinary-extraction">4</a> to $F^{(m)}$ with the integer parameter $k'=\lceil mr/50\rceil$. For sufficiently large $m$, <a href="#small:blowup-lower" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="small:blowup-lower">[small:blowup-lower]</a> exceeds $7k'$. We obtain a $k'$-connected subgraph $J$ with $$\chi(J)\ge\chi(F^{(m)})-6k'
 >\frac{19mr}{50}-6
 >\frac{31mr}{100}.$$ Each restricted separator of the decomposition has fewer than $r/100$ vertices, so its blow-up has fewer than $mr/100<k'$ vertices. Thus $J$ cannot meet both exclusive sides of any such split: deleting its vertices in the separator would disconnect $J$ with fewer than $k'$ deletions. Nor can $J$ be contained in the separator, because its order is greater than $k'$. Descending the decomposition places $J$ inside a single blown-up leaf restriction, contradicting that leaf’s coloring bound.

It follows that some $k$-connected leaf satisfies <a href="#small:region-expectation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="small:region-expectation">[small:region-expectation]</a>. This argument also covers the case where $P$ is too small to be $k$-connected: if all leaves were small, the same contradiction would apply. Finally, the blow-up is only an auxiliary graph for the extraction theorem, which requires no minor exclusion; no bound on its clique-minor number was used. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-12"></a>
#### Private models and a connected complement

Assume the failure hypothesis of Lemma <a href="#small:fixed-region" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="small:fixed-region">12</a>, and fix the resulting subgraph $H$. Sample $q$ fresh independent copies $W_1,\ldots,W_q$ of <a href="#small:remainder" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="small:remainder">[small:remainder]</a>. Put $$T_i=V(H)\cap\left(W_i\setminus\bigcup_{j\ne i}W_j\right),
 \qquad
 U=V(H)\cap\bigcup_{i=1}^qW_i.$$ The sets $T_i$ are pairwise disjoint subsets of $U$.

<a id="stmt-small-private"></a>
<div id="small:private" class="lemma">

**Lemma 13**. *With failure probability at most $4q(q-1)p+o(1)$, every $H[T_i]$ has fractional chromatic number greater than $r/8$, and hence contains a $K_{2x}$ model.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-small-private"><summary>Proof of stmt-small-private</summary>

*Proof.* By <a href="#small:region-expectation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="small:region-expectation">[small:region-expectation]</a> and Lemma <a href="#small:concentration" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="small:concentration">11</a>, the events $$\mathcal A_i=\{f(H[W_i\cap V(H)])>r/5\}$$ all hold with probability $1-o(1)$: the individual failure probability is at most $2\exp(-t^{7/10})$, and $q\le Q_0(\log t)^2$.

For each outcome of $W_i$ satisfying $\mathcal A_i$, choose optimal dual weights on $H[W_i\cap V(H)]$ of total weight $a_i>r/5$. Choose these weights as a function of $W_i$ alone. Conditional on this one copy, each other copy still satisfies the vertex survival bound <a href="#small:survival" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="small:survival">[small:survival]</a>. Therefore the expected weight on vertices belonging to some other copy is at most $(q-1)pa_i$. Markov’s inequality shows that the probability of $\mathcal A_i$ together with the loss of more than $a_i/4$ is at most $4(q-1)p$.

Taking a union bound over $i$, we conclude that, except with probability $4q(q-1)p+o(1)$, all private sets retain weight at least $3a_i/4>3r/20>r/8$.
